summaries.example: Imagine two dice being rolled. There are 36 ways they might land. Only two ways make the total 11: 5 and 6, or 6 and 5. The dice have these possible ways of landing even before the roll. A possible state of affairs is one way things could be, whether or not it actually happens.
summaries.summary: A state of affairs is a possible way for things to be. For example, a die showing six is one possible state of the die, even if the die shows another number. Philosophers compare states of affairs with thoughts and facts. Thoughts are things we can believe and that can be true or false. Facts are what make truths true. States of affairs are meant to help explain possibility, probability, and sometimes what we perceive or value. A state of affairs can exist without happening, which makes it different from a fact. It also involves actual objects and properties more directly than a thought does. The entry explains several ideas about how states of affairs are put together and what makes them one unified thing. It does not present one final answer to every question.
key_ideas: States of affairs describe ways objects and properties can go together.
A state of affairs can exist as a possibility even when it does not happen.
Thoughts can be true or false, while states of affairs obtain or fail to obtain.
Facts and states of affairs are related, but philosophers usually give them different jobs.
Philosophers disagree about exactly how objects and properties are united in a state of affairs.
summaries.why_it_matters: The idea helps philosophers talk carefully about possibilities. It lets them ask not only what is true now, but also what could have happened, what might happen, and how likely different outcomes are. It also shows why everyday words such as “fact,” “thought,” and “possibility” may point to different ideas.

important_terms.definition: A way things could be. It may happen, or it may fail to happen, but it is still something we can consider.
A thing that makes a thought or sentence true. For example, the fact that a tree is green helps make “The tree is green” true.
The meaning or content of a belief, wish, or sentence. A thought can be true or false.
When a state of affairs really happens or is the way things are.

questions_to_think_about: Is a way something could happen the same as a thought about it?
Can something be a possibility even if it never happens?
When you see a bent-looking stick in water, are you seeing the stick, a state of affairs, or both?

summaries.example: Consider the sentences “Hesperus shines” and “Phosphorus shines.” Hesperus and Phosphorus are two names for the same planet, so the sentences can concern the same state of affairs even though someone might believe one sentence without believing the other. By contrast, the sentences present different thoughts if their modes of presentation differ. This illustrates why states of affairs may be less finely individuated than thoughts while still being more informative than mere truth-values.
summaries.summary: The entry examines whether states of affairs are needed in addition to thoughts and facts. A state of affairs is presented as a complex involving objects and properties, and it may exist whether or not it obtains. This feature gives states of affairs a central role in accounts of possibility, probability, and modality. Thoughts, by contrast, are contents of propositional attitudes such as belief and are often distinguished by their modes of presentation. Thus, someone may accept one description of an object while rejecting another, even when the descriptions concern the same object. Facts are commonly introduced as truth-makers: they are actual complexes whose existence is supposed to guarantee the truth of a proposition. States of affairs cannot simply be identified with facts, because non-obtaining states of affairs are part of the intended theory. The entry also discusses using states of affairs to construct possible worlds, to analyze perception and value, and to understand counterfactual reasoning. A major remaining challenge is the unity problem: what unifies constituents into one state of affairs? Proposed answers appeal to external unifiers, internal structure, functions, or predicability. None is presented as decisively established.
key_ideas: States of affairs are proposed as a distinct category: they can exist without obtaining and involve objects and properties directly.
Their possible or probable status gives them a role that thoughts and facts may not fill as well.
Thoughts are often more finely individuated than states of affairs because different descriptions can support different beliefs.
Facts are used in truth-maker theories, whereas states of affairs are especially useful in theories of modality and possible worlds.
The unity problem asks what makes objects and properties form one state of affairs rather than a mere collection.
One proposed answer appeals to predicability and ontological dependence, but the entry treats the issue as unresolved.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction matters because philosophical explanations need different kinds of objects for different jobs. Thoughts help explain belief and linguistic meaning; facts help explain why truths are true; states of affairs help represent possibilities, including possibilities that are not actual. Studying their differences also exposes deeper questions about reference, modality, perception, value, and how complex entities are formed.

important_terms.definition: A possible way objects and properties are arranged or related, whether or not that way is actual.
An entity proposed to guarantee the truth of a truth-bearer; facts are often offered as truth-makers.
The content of a belief, desire, or assertion, capable of being true or false and often understood through a mode of presentation.
A truth-bearing complex involving objects and properties; unlike a merely possible state of affairs, a fact is actual.
The status of a state of affairs when it is actually the case.
A way an object or property is presented in thought, which can differ even when the same object is involved.
A complete way things might be. Some philosophers analyze possible worlds as maximal possible states of affairs; others treat them as concrete worlds or other abstract constructions.
A relation in which the identity or existence of one thing depends on another, without necessarily containing that other thing as a part.

questions_to_think_about: If two sentences have the same truth-value, must they refer to the same thought or state of affairs?
Can a non-obtaining state of affairs be a genuine object of thought without being a fact?
Does a theory of possible worlds explain modality, or does it already presuppose possibility?
What should distinguish the state of affairs that Romeo loves Juliet from the state of affairs that Juliet loves Romeo?
Are experiences of illusion best explained by a state of affairs that exists but does not obtain?

summaries.example: Suppose your class is planning a picnic. Several outcomes are possible: it rains, it stays sunny, or it is sunny but windy. The sunny-and-windy outcome is a possible state of affairs even before anyone knows whether it will happen. If it really happens, it obtains. A thought is different: one student may believe “the picnic will be sunny,” while another may believe “the picnic will be sunny and windy.” Their beliefs can differ even if the same possible situation is being discussed.
summaries.summary: The entry asks what states of affairs are and why philosophers might need them. A state of affairs is a possible way for objects and properties to be connected. It can exist as a possibility even when it does not actually happen. This separates it from a fact, which is normally understood as something actual and truth-making. It also separates it from a thought, which is the content of belief, desire, or another attitude and can depend on how something is described. For example, two names may refer to the same object while producing different thoughts for a person. States of affairs are especially useful in probability and modal reasoning. When we calculate the chances of dice outcomes, we consider possible ways the dice might land, including ways that do not occur. Some philosophers use such states to explain possible worlds, while other theories understand possible worlds differently. The entry also considers perception, value, and the difficult question of what unifies the objects and properties in a state of affairs. It presents several proposals but leaves important disagreements open.
key_ideas: A state of affairs is a possible situation, not merely a sentence or a belief about that situation.
States of affairs may exist as possibilities even when they do not obtain.
Thoughts are connected to belief and desire, so two different descriptions can lead to different thoughts.
Facts are usually treated as actual and are often used to explain truth.
States of affairs are useful for thinking about probability: possible outcomes can have different chances.
Philosophers disagree about whether states of affairs are basic objects, constructions, or something else.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us separate three questions: What do we think or say? What is actually true? What could be true? Keeping these questions apart can clarify discussions about chance, alternate possibilities, mistakes in perception, and what makes something valuable. It also teaches an important philosophical lesson: a useful idea may still have difficult unanswered questions.

important_terms.definition: A way for objects and properties to be arranged; it may happen or fail to happen.
Something actual that helps explain why a true claim is true.
The content of what someone believes, wants, or says; it can be true or false.
To be the way things really are; a state of affairs obtains when it is actual.
A feature that makes one description or way of thinking different from another description of the same object.
A complete way the world could be. Some philosophers understand one as a maximal possible state of affairs.

questions_to_think_about: Is “the picnic is sunny” the same thing as the thought that the picnic is sunny? Why might they differ?
Why might a philosopher need possibilities that do not become actual?
Could two sentences be true but describe different states of affairs?
What makes a group of objects and properties one unified situation?
Should an illusion count as awareness of a state of affairs that does not obtain?
